name: Emergence
aliases: The whole is more than the sum of its parts
statement: A whole can have properties its parts lack, arising from how they interact: the whole exceeds the sum of its parts.
statementAccent: the whole exceeds the sum of its parts
meaning: Emergence is the phenomenon in which a complex system or whole exhibits properties, behaviors, or patterns that its individual parts do not have on their own, and that arise from the interactions among those parts. It is often summed up in the phrase that the whole is more than the sum of its parts. Emergent properties are typically novel and often not obviously predictable from knowledge of the parts alone. Standard illustrations include the wetness of water, which is not a property of individual water molecules; the coordinated behavior of an ant colony or a flock of birds; temperature and pressure arising from molecular motion; and, more controversially, consciousness arising from neurons. A central distinction is between weak and strong emergence. Weak emergence, as formulated by Mark Bedau, describes properties that arise from the parts and their interactions and are in principle derivable from the lower level, though perhaps only through simulation, so they are surprising but not metaphysically novel and are consistent with physicalism. Strong emergence describes properties that are genuinely novel and irreducible, not deducible even in principle from the lower-level properties, and that may exert downward causation on the parts; strong emergence is more metaphysically robust and far more controversial. The concept has a history in nineteenth-century thought and British Emergentism, and it is central to philosophy of mind, philosophy of science, and complexity theory.
mechanism: Emergence describes a relationship in which a higher-level property depends on lower-level parts and their organization yet is in some sense autonomous from them. The parts interact according to their own rules, and out of these interactions the whole comes to display features that none of the parts possesses individually and that characterize only the collective. How radical this autonomy is distinguishes two kinds of emergence. In weak emergence, the higher-level property is fully determined by and, in principle, derivable from the lower-level facts, so it is consistent with physicalism and the causal closure of the physical; it counts as emergent because the derivation may be possible only by tracing the interactions step by step, often through simulation, so the property is unexpected and its explanation cannot be shortened, as Bedau puts it, but it involves no new fundamental ingredient. In strong emergence, the higher-level property is held to be genuinely novel and not deducible even in principle from the lower-level laws and properties; it is taken to have novel causal powers of its own and often to exert downward causation, influencing the very parts from which it arises. Strong emergence would be inconsistent with the completeness of physics and is therefore metaphysically robust and controversial. The two notions apply the same intuitive idea, that wholes can have properties their parts lack, with very different commitments about reducibility and causation.

examples.text: Wetness is a property of collections of water molecules interacting, not of any single molecule, a familiar emergent property.
Weak emergence is derivable in principle from the parts, perhaps only by simulation, while strong emergence is held to be irreducible.
The coordinated patterns of an ant colony or a flock of birds emerge from simple local interactions among the individuals.

variants.name: Weak emergence
variants.text: Bedau's notion of properties derivable in principle from the parts, often only by simulation, consistent with physicalism.

variants.name: Strong emergence
variants.text: The controversial notion of genuinely novel, irreducible properties with downward causation, inconsistent with the completeness of physics.

whyItMatters: Emergence is a central concept across philosophy and science, providing a way to understand how complexity and novelty arise from the interactions of simpler parts. It occupies a valuable middle ground between reductionism, which explains everything in terms of fundamental parts, and dualism, which posits wholly separate realms, by allowing that higher-level properties depend on lower-level ones yet display genuine novelty and a degree of autonomy. The concept is indispensable in the philosophy of science and in complexity theory, systems theory, and the special sciences, where it illuminates how phenomena like life, temperature, ecosystems, economies, and social patterns arise from and yet transcend their underlying constituents. In the philosophy of mind, emergence frames one of the most important questions about consciousness, whether the mind is weakly emergent from the brain, and so in principle explicable, or strongly emergent and irreducible, a question tied to the hard problem and to debates over physicalism. The distinction between weak and strong emergence sharpens these debates by separating the scientifically respectable claim that complex behavior can be surprising and hard to derive from the far bolder claim that new fundamental properties come into being. As the concept of wholes exceeding their parts, emergence is fundamental to understanding complexity.

working.text: have many parts interact according to their own local rules within a system.
observe the whole display novel properties or behaviors that none of the parts has alone.
distinguish weak emergence, derivable in principle from the parts, from strong emergence, held to be irreducible.

limits: Emergence is a valuable concept, but strong emergence in particular is controversial and should not be presented as established. Critics argue that strong emergence may be incoherent, since a property cannot easily be both dependent on the base and yet fundamentally novel, and that there is little or no clear evidence for genuinely new causal powers, with Brian McLaughlin famously saying there is not a scintilla of evidence for them; reductionists are skeptical that strong emergence occurs at all. Weak emergence, by contrast, is widely accepted as scientifically respectable but faces the charge that it adds little beyond the recognition that complex systems can be hard to predict. Whether consciousness is weakly or strongly emergent from the brain is a genuinely open and contested question, not a settled example, and even the familiar cases like the wetness of water are sometimes disputed as illustrations. So emergence robustly captures how wholes can have properties their parts lack, understood as a concept whose weak form is accepted but whose strong form, and its application to consciousness, remain deeply contested.
misreadings: Emergence does not always mean that new fundamental properties come into being; weak emergence, the widely accepted kind, is fully derivable in principle from the parts, while only the controversial strong emergence claims genuine irreducibility. It is not established that consciousness is strongly emergent, which is an open and contested question rather than a settled example. And strong emergence is not a demonstrated fact, since critics doubt its coherence and evidence, so treating all emergence as producing new fundamental properties, consciousness as clearly strongly emergent, or strong emergence as established, misreads a concept whose strong form is deeply contested.
origin: The phenomenon in which wholes have properties their parts lack, arising from their interactions, with roots in J. S. Mill and British Emergentism and the term coined by G. H. Lewes in 1875; central to philosophy of mind, science, and complexity.
